\chapter{The Body, Further Down --- Arm, Leg, Foot, Tooth, Ear}
\label{ch:brazo-y-pie}
\hlchaptermodality{314}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the arm, the leg, the foot, the tooth and the hearing in Spanish.}

Complete ES-C314-oido: name all five in order, from the arm at the top to the hearing you cannot point at.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el brazo]{el brazo — the arm that was only ever the shorter one}

\label{lesson:ES-C314-brazo}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before a new run starts. Which of your five answers refuses to change for a woman? (\emph{Triste} — it ends in \emph{-e}.) And which one means your hands are full? (\emph{Ocupado}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la mano — one end of it.
  \item el hombro — the other end.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{BRA-zo}, two beats, stress on the first. The \emph{r} is a single tap against the ridge behind your teeth. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el brazo} — \textquotedblleft{}the arm.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{brakhion} was a comparative. It meant \textquotedblleft{}the shorter one.\textquotedblright{} Greek anatomists used it for the upper arm — the shorter half of the limb — and the name stuck to a body part for a reason nobody feels any more.

Latin borrowed it as \textbf{bracchium} and dropped the comparison entirely. By the time Spanish had it, \emph{brazo} was the whole arm, shoulder to hand.

English holds three pieces of it. A \textbf{brace} was armour for the arm before it was anything that holds a thing steady. A \textbf{bracelet} is a little \emph{brace}. And to \textbf{embrace} somebody is to put them \emph{in} your arms: \emph{em-} is \emph{in}, and \emph{brace} is this word.

So \emph{el hombro}, then \emph{el brazo}, then \emph{la mano}. You have the whole limb now, top to bottom.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five more of the body begin here.

The first three walk you from the shoulder to the ground; the last two are smaller and harder to point at.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el brazo}
  \item \emph{el brazo y la mano}
  \item \emph{el hombro}, then \emph{el brazo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{brakhion} mean before it meant an arm? (The shorter one.) And what are you doing when you \emph{embrace} somebody? (Putting them in your arms.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la pierna]{la pierna — a ham, put back on the body}

\label{lesson:ES-C314-pierna}



\begin{quote}
Which English word is \emph{bracchium}, worn down and put on a wrist? (\emph{Bracelet}.) And why does \emph{triste} not change for a woman? (It ends in \emph{-e}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el brazo — the same idea, upper storey.
  \item la rodilla — the hinge in the middle of this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PIER-na}, two beats. The \emph{ie} is one slide, not two vowels. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la pierna} — \textquotedblleft{}the leg.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{perna} was a ham. Not a leg: a \emph{cut}. The haunch of a pig, salted and hung from a beam. Spanish took the butcher's word and put it back on the living body — which is the opposite of the usual direction, where a piece of an animal gets named after the human part it resembles.

Watch the \emph{e} break to \emph{ie} on the way: \emph{perna} becomes \emph{pierna}. That is the same crack you tracked through \emph{cielo}, \emph{miel} and \emph{piel}. A stressed \emph{e} in Latin, an \emph{ie} in Spanish, every time.

Spanish is nearly alone in using this word. Italian says \emph{gamba} and French says \emph{jambe}, both from Late Latin \textbf{camba}, a hock. English quietly holds that one instead: the \textbf{jamb} of a door is its leg, and to \textbf{gambol} is to kick yours about.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of the limb, and a second sighting of the \emph{ie} crack.

\emph{Piel}, \emph{pierna}: put an \emph{e} back where the \emph{ie} is and the Latin usually shows itself. It will happen twice more before this chapter is out.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la pierna}
  \item \emph{la pierna y la rodilla}
  \item \emph{el brazo}, then \emph{la pierna}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{perna}? (A ham — the cut.) What happened to its \emph{e}? (It broke into \emph{ie}.) And which English door-part is the other Latin word for a leg? (The \emph{jamb}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el pie]{el pie — one syllable, and half the world says it}

\label{lesson:ES-C314-pie}



\begin{quote}
Which body part is a ham? (\emph{La pierna}.) And what is \emph{em-brace} doing, literally? (Putting somebody in your arms.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la pierna — what this one is on the end of.
  \item el tobillo — the joint just above it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PIE}, one beat. Two letters of vowel, one slide, no second syllable. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pie} — \textquotedblleft{}the foot.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{pedem} — and \emph{pedem} goes back a very long way before Latin. The root under it is \emph{ped-}, and it is one of the oldest things anybody can reconstruct: old enough that it survives, recognisably, across most of Europe and a good part of Asia.

English took it three separate times.

Through Latin: \textbf{pedal}, \textbf{pedestrian}, \textbf{pedestal}, and \textbf{pedigree}, which is French \emph{pied de grue}, \textquotedblleft{}a crane's foot\textquotedblright{} — the three-line mark that shows descent on a family tree.

Through Greek, where \emph{ped-} had become \emph{pod-}: \textbf{podium}, \textbf{tripod}, \textbf{octopus}.

And through Germanic, where an old sound shift turned every \emph{p} into an \emph{f}: \textbf{foot}.

So \emph{pie}, \emph{foot}, \emph{podium} and \emph{pedal} are four faces of one word.

It reaches further than Europe. Hindi says \emph{pair}. Persian says \emph{pa}. Those are not borrowings from anybody — they are cousins, descended in parallel from the same root, and they have been apart for perhaps five thousand years.

Latin \emph{pedem} lost its ending and broke its \emph{e}, exactly as \emph{perna} did.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The bottom of the body, and the widest-travelled word you have met.

Most words here connect Spanish to English. This one connects Spanish to Hindi and Persian as well.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el pie}
  \item \emph{el tobillo y el pie}
  \item \emph{la pierna}, then \emph{el pie}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English word is \emph{ped-} after the Germanic \emph{p} turned to \emph{f}? (\emph{Foot}.) What is a \emph{pedigree} named after? (A crane's foot.) And name one language outside Europe that kept the root. (Hindi \emph{pair}, or Persian \emph{pa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el diente]{el diente — the tooth in the dandelion}

\label{lesson:ES-C314-diente}



\begin{quote}
Which one word is Spanish, Hindi and Persian all at once? (\emph{Pie}.) And what was a \emph{perna}? (A ham.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la boca — where these live.
  \item el dolor — what sends you to somebody about one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{DIEN-te}, two beats. The \emph{d} is soft, tongue against the very teeth it names. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el diente} — \textquotedblleft{}the tooth.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{dentem}, and the \emph{e} breaks to \emph{ie} one more time. That is the fourth time in two chapters. It is not a coincidence and it is not a list to memorise — it is one rule, doing its work.

English has the Latin form wherever teeth are being discussed carefully: \textbf{dental}, \textbf{dentist}, \textbf{denture}. It also has it where nobody notices. To \textbf{indent} a line is to put a \emph{tooth} in the margin. A \textbf{dent} in a car door is a tooth-mark.

And then there is the flower. French called it \emph{dent de lion}, \textquotedblleft{}lion's tooth\textquotedblright{}, for the row of jagged points down each leaf. English heard the French and wrote it down the way it sounded: \textbf{dandelion}.

Meanwhile Germanic did to \emph{dent-} exactly what it did to \emph{ped-}. The \emph{d} softened, the ending wore away, and out came \textbf{tooth}. \emph{Diente} and \emph{tooth} are the same word, two sound shifts apart — the same trick you saw one lesson ago with \emph{pie} and \emph{foot}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four of the body, and a second matched pair.

\emph{Pie} and \emph{foot}. \emph{Diente} and \emph{tooth}. Once you can hear that shift, the Germanic half of English stops looking unrelated to the Latin half.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el diente}
  \item \emph{la boca y el diente}
  \item \emph{el pie}, then \emph{el diente}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a dandelion named for? (A lion's tooth — the jagged leaf.) What does \emph{indent} put in the margin? (A tooth.) And which English word is \emph{diente} after the Germanic shift? (\emph{Tooth}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el oído]{el oído — the hearing, made into a thing}

\label{lesson:ES-C314-oido}



\begin{quote}
What is a dandelion? (A lion's tooth.) And which Spanish word do Hindi and Persian also say? (\emph{Pie}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item oír — the verb this is the past participle of.
  \item la garganta — another part you cannot see.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{o-Í-do}, three beats. The accent on the \emph{í} holds the \emph{o} and the \emph{í} apart, so this is not a diphthong. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el oído} — \textquotedblleft{}the ear,\textquotedblright{} or more exactly, \textquotedblleft{}the hearing.\textquotedblright{}

You already have the verb \emph{oír}, \textquotedblleft{}to hear.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Oído} is its past participle — \textquotedblleft{}heard\textquotedblright{} — and Spanish has taken that participle and stood it up as a noun.

So \emph{el oído} is not the flap on the side of your head. Spanish has a separate word for that. \emph{El oído} is the inner ear and the sense itself: the hearing, the thing that works or does not.

Under both of them sits Latin \textbf{audire}, one of the most productive roots English owns. \textbf{Audio} is \textquotedblleft{}I hear.\textquotedblright{} An \textbf{audience} is a hearing. An \textbf{audition} is a hearing. An \textbf{auditorium} is a room for hearing in. An \textbf{auditor} checks accounts by \emph{listening} to them read aloud, which is how it was done before most people could read.

The best of them is \textbf{obedient}. It is \emph{ob-audire}: to listen \emph{toward} somebody. Obedience, in Latin, was never more than paying close attention.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five of the body, and the chapter closes.

Four of them you can point at. The fifth is a faculty — and it is the one carrying the largest family in English.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el oído}
  \item \emph{el diente}, then \emph{el oído}
  \item \emph{el brazo, la pierna, el pie, el diente, el oído}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What part of speech was \emph{oído} before it was a noun? (A past participle — \textquotedblleft{}heard\textquotedblright{}.) What is an \emph{auditor} doing, in the old sense? (Listening to the accounts read aloud.) And what is \emph{obedient}, taken apart? (Listening toward somebody.)
\end{tcolorbox}
